title: Missing HttpOnly Flag on CSRF Token Cookie
description:
The CSRF token cookie (csrftoken) is missing the HttpOnly flag, making it accessible to JavaScript running in the browser. While the CSRF token itself is not meant to be secret (it's transmitted in the response and form), making it accessible to JavaScript allows for potential XSS-based CSRF attacks. An attacker could use reflected XSS to inject JavaScript that reads the CSRF token via document.cookie, then use it to perform CSRF attacks on authenticated users.

The vulnerability exists because the Django application does not set the CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY configuration option to True. This allows any JavaScript code executing in the browser context (whether legitimate or injected via XSS) to read the CSRF token value using document.cookie, which can then be used to construct forged requests with valid CSRF tokens.

While the CSRF token's value being public is not itself a vulnerability (CSRF tokens are meant to be sent with requests), the accessible nature creates an additional attack vector when combined with XSS vulnerabilities, as it allows an attacker to reliably obtain a valid CSRF token for authenticated users.
impact:
If an XSS vulnerability exists on the application or related domains, an attacker could potentially:
1. Read the CSRF token via JavaScript (document.cookie)
2. Use the token value to construct forged requests with valid CSRF tokens
3. Perform state-changing actions (POST/PUT/DELETE) on behalf of authenticated users
4. Bypass the CSRF protection mechanism that relies on the token being difficult to obtain

While standard CSRF attacks wouldn't normally work against this application due to CSRF protection, the missing HttpOnly flag exposes an additional attack vector when combined with XSS. This is particularly concerning given the existing Stored XSS vulnerability documented in the registration flow.

Business impact: Account compromise, unauthorized actions (payment, profile changes), data modification
evidence:
POC execution confirmed the vulnerability:

Set-Cookie header captured:
```
Set-Cookie:  csrftoken=vPIQS40zY4HVeB7TAYjcVFUeAYXFUQuY; expires=Mon, 30 Nov 2026 16:10:38 GMT; Max-Age=31449600; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
```

Analysis of cookie attributes:
- ✓ Present: expires, Max-Age, Path, SameSite
- ✗ MISSING: HttpOnly flag
- ✗ MISSING: Secure flag (expected on localhost, required for production)

The absence of "HttpOnly" in the Set-Cookie header confirms that JavaScript running in the browser can access the CSRF token via document.cookie.

Test command: `curl http://localhost:8081/accounts/login/ -i | grep "Set-Cookie"`
remediation:
1. Enable HttpOnly flag on CSRF token cookie in Django settings:
   - Open settings.py
   - Add or modify: `CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True`

2. For production environments, also set:
   - `CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True` (ensures cookie only sent over HTTPS)
   - This is already configured with SameSite=Lax which is acceptable

3. Verify the complete recommended configuration:
   ```python
   CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True
   CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True  # production only
   CSRF_COOKIE_SAMESITE = 'Lax'  # already set
   ```

4. After changes, restart the Django application

5. Verify the fix:
   - Access login page again
   - Check Set-Cookie headers with curl
   - Confirm "HttpOnly" attribute is now present in the csrftoken cookie header

6. Test that CSRF protection still functions correctly after changes
references:
CWE-1004: Sensitive Cookie Without 'HttpOnly' Flag (https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1004.html)
CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without 'Secure' Attribute (https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/614.html)
OWASP A05:2021 - Security Misconfiguration
OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
Django CSRF Protection Documentation: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/csrf/
